1:
Calvin objects to the chapter break before reaching the verse. Whoever made the division improperly separated this paragraph from the preceding, since it is nothing else than the concluding section in which Paul explains the difference between us and the ancient people, by a third comparison drawn from a minor's relation to his tutor. Luther attends to the same strategy, remarking on the vehement affection with which Paul calls the Galatians back, gathering similitudes from experience, from Abraham, from the Scriptures and from time; ignorant people, he adds, are sooner persuaded with similitudes than with subtle disputations, and will rather behold an image well painted than a book well written, so Paul lies in wait with a certain holy subtlety to take them unawares. Henry gives the point of the figure, that the Old Testament church was a child under age, a dispensation of grace yet comparatively one of darkness and bondage.

The two officials in the second verse produce a four-way disagreement. Ellicott makes it a distinction between guardians of the person and stewards of the property. Calvin, quoting Chandler, reverses it: the first properly signifies the preceptor or tutor, the second the guardian who takes care of his person and estate. Clarke calls the words nearly similar and glosses the first as executor and the second as the one who superintends the family estate, such as we call trustee. Wesley divides them in six words, one as to his person and the other as to his substance.

Barnes and Robertson work from usage and both loosen it. Barnes warns that tutor with us means instructor, which is not the sense, the Greek properly meaning steward or manager: one, usually a slave or freedman, to whose care the boys were committed. The second he makes a house-manager over the servants and the accounts, commonly a slave rewarded with the office, having charge of the sons in pecuniary matters. Then he withdraws the precision, saying it is not necessary to mark the difference with great accuracy. Robertson reports the papyri, where the first is frequent as guardian of an orphan minor and the second as estate manager and treasurer, and states a gap in the evidence: no example is known of the second used of one in charge of a minor, and none where both occur together. He passes on Burton's argument that no legal distinction is meant, the terms designating two functions of one person, and judges the point does not disturb Paul's illustration.

The clause about the time appointed sets Ellicott and Barnes against each other. Barnes takes it as a plain statement of the father's power: our law fixes twenty-one and other countries other times, but the time when the son inherits is fixed by the father if living or by his will if dead, so the son cannot claim the property merely on coming of age. Ellicott denies that this held in Greek or Roman law, and dismisses the suggestion of larger paternal powers in Galatia as a subtlety in which learning overreaches itself, the Apostle's short sojourn being unlikely to have acquainted him with the local code. His solution is that the application of the analogy has modified its statement: the minority of the race is fixed by the heavenly Father, though an earthly father must conform to a law not his own. Robertson supplies the detail neither disputes, that under Roman law the guardian had charge until fourteen and the curator until twenty-five, Ramsay reporting the same in Graeco-Phrygian cities except that a father in Syria appointed both officers where a Roman appointed only the first. Gill adds from the rabbins that guardians were chosen not from women or servants but from men of substance and wisdom. Luther closes on the purpose of the restraint, that this subjection is very profitable for the heir, who would otherwise through folly soon waste all his goods.
3:
Who the we includes is disputed three against three. Gill restricts it to the Jews, since of such the apostle is only speaking, having addressed the Gentiles separately just before. Barnes limits it the same way against Bloomfield, on two grounds: the heathen in no sense sustained such a relation to the law and the promises, and the wider reading is not pertinent to Paul's design. Clarke agrees, taking it of the whole Jewish people. Ellicott admits the Jews in the first instance but includes the Gentiles, since the Apostle speaks from the Christian point of view, meaning all who are now Christians whatever their antecedents; what is said of the law of Moses applies more faintly to the law of conscience and of nature. Robertson glosses it as Jews and Gentiles, Wesley as the church of God.

The phrase rendered elements of the world is harder, and every voice starts from the same etymology and lands differently. Barnes traces the word to a row or series, then a pin or peg such as the gnomon of a dial, then anything elementary like a sound or a letter, the New Testament applying it both to the first principles of religion and to the parts of the physical world. Robertson lists the same range, adds that the papyri illustrate every variety, records that some argue here for the heavenly bodies, points to Burton's excursus, and follows Lightfoot in taking Paul to mean the rudimentary character of the law for Jews and Gentiles alike.

Ellicott alone records what the tradition used to say. The older commentators mostly took the word of the elements of nature, the heavenly bodies, either as objects of Gentile worship or as marking the Jewish festivals; but he judges the other sense best, the rudiments of religious teaching, called worldly because mundane and material, including no clear recognition of spiritual things. Calvin sets out the same alternative briefly, that the word may mean outward and bodily things or metaphorically rudiments, and prefers the latter; things of spiritual signification are called worldly because the truth was not enjoyed in a simple form but involved in earthly figures, so that what was outward must have been of the world, though a heavenly mystery lay concealed under it.

Clarke and Wesley both reach for the alphabet, and Clarke builds it into an argument. He calls the expression a mere Jewish phrase for the principles of this world, and holds the law was not the science of salvation but only its alphabet, which in the Gospel is composed into a most glorious system of divine knowledge. As the alphabet is nothing of itself unless compounded into syllables and words, so the law by itself gives no salvation; it contains the outlines of the Gospel, but the Gospel alone fills them up. Wesley puts the same figure in a phrase, that the typical observances were like the first elements of grammar, the A B C of children, and so gross as hardly to carry our thoughts beyond this world.

Luther reads the verse as custody with hope in it. When we were little children we were heirs, having the promise of the inheritance to come; but because the fulness of time was not yet come, Moses our schoolmaster held us in captivity with our hands bound, so that we could bear no rule nor possess our inheritance. Yet as an heir is nourished in hope of the liberty to come, so Moses nourished us with the hope of the promise to be revealed at the time appointed. He distinguishes two ways in which the time of the law ends: by the coming of Christ in the flesh at the time appointed, and in that the same Christ comes to us daily and hourly in spirit, since though he sanctified all at once with his own blood, we are not yet perfectly pure.
4:
Why the coming was delayed divides two men sharply. Barnes puts the question and admits defeat: it is often asked why four thousand dark and gloomy years were allowed to roll on while the world sank deeper in sin, and to this perhaps no satisfactory answer can be given, though God undoubtedly saw reasons we cannot see. Calvin forbids the enquiry: at what time it was expedient that the Son should be revealed belonged to God alone to judge, and this ought to restrain all curiosity, so that no man dispute why Christ did not appear sooner. Gill answers by dating rather than reasoning, placing the time in the covenant between God and his Son and fixing it before the civil government ceased from Judah, particularly in the seventy weeks; and the Jews themselves, he notes, own the time to be fixed and hold the Messiah shall come at it whether they are worthy or not. Ellicott draws a structural conclusion, that we have here a clear expression of religion as progressive, divided into periods and culminating in Christianity.

The clause about the woman produces the sharpest split. Clarke reads the miraculous conception straight out of it, the Son produced by the power of God in the womb of the Virgin without any intervention of man, and Wesley the same, made miraculously of the substance of a virgin without the concurrence of a man. Ellicott denies it flatly: the phrase is better translated born of a woman, there is no allusion here to the miraculous conception, the expression was of common use, and it brings out not the divinity but the true humanity of Christ. Robertson agrees that there is no direct reference here to the Virgin Birth, the words meaning simply coming from a woman as all men do; but he adds that the deity had just been affirmed by the words his Son, so both natures stand together, and that the fact of the Virgin Birth agrees perfectly with language that does not assert it.

Two older voices argue about the same word from the other side. Cyril of Jerusalem attacks two errors at once, refusing to endure heretics who teach Christ's coming as a phantom and abhorring equally those who say the Saviour's birth was of husband and wife, calling him the child of Joseph and Mary because it is written that he took unto him his wife; his answer is from usage, that as Rachel was called Jacob's wife before the wedded state merely on a promise, so Mary was called the wife of Joseph because she had been betrothed. Luther meets the objection that Paul seems almost in reproach to call the Virgin only a woman, which was not well taken even by some ancient doctors; his defence is that Paul is treating the highest and principal matter of all. He also finds the whole of Christology here, the person in God sent his Son born of a woman and the office in made under the law to redeem them under the law.

Whom the redemption reaches is where Gill parts from the rest: Christ was not sent to redeem all that were under the law, for though all mankind were included in it as a covenant of works with Adam, only some out of every kindred, tongue and nation are redeemed, even all the elect. Calvin turns adoption into a polemic, holding that the fathers were certain of their adoption but did not so fully enjoy it, and that those who now burden the church with ceremonies defraud her of the just right of adoption. Luther asks by what merit the blessing was received and answers by none at all, freely and utterly unworthy, yet not without merit, since the merit is Christ's. Ellicott adds that the pre-existence of the Son is distinctly recognised here, and that redemption is followed by adoption.
6:
The opening conjunction carries the argument. Calvin makes it strictly evidential: the adoption must have preceded the testimony given by the Holy Spirit, but the effect is the sign of the cause, so that in venturing to call God your Father you have the direction of the Spirit of Christ, and it is therefore certain that you are sons; the Spirit, he adds, is the earnest and pledge of adoption. Ellicott keeps the causal sense on balance while noting the conjunction may possibly mean in proof that, and puts the substance as filial emotion, since it is not you that speak but the Spirit of Christ, who prompts your prayers. Robertson settles it as causal and adds that we were sons in God's elective purpose and love. Gill defines the sonship by exclusion: not in so high a sense as Christ is Son, nor so low as all men are God's offspring, nor as magistrates are called children of the most High, nor merely by profession, but by adoption owing to free and sovereign grace.

Whose Spirit is meant divides them, and Barnes stands alone. The spirit referred to, he says, does not mean the Holy Spirit as such, nor its miraculous endowments, but the spirit which made them like the Lord Jesus and by which they were enabled to approach God as his children; the exalted Son had the spirit appropriate to that relation, and the adopted have the same. Robertson identifies it plainly as the Holy Spirit, called elsewhere the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of Jesus Christ, and proceeding from the Father and the Son. Cyril of Jerusalem argues the same identity from the titles, that the Holy Spirit and the Comforter are the same, that the Comforter is the Spirit of Truth, and that he is called both the Spirit of God and the Spirit of the Father, so that one and the same is meant under different names.

Clarke reads the verse as trinitarian and numbers the persons in an order of his own: God the Father he calls the first person of the glorious Trinity, the Spirit sent forth the second person, and the Son whose Spirit it is the third; the cry of Abba he treats as the fullest evidence that Father, Son and Spirit had become their portion.

The doubled address gets three explanations. Ellicott calls it a reduplication of loving entreaty and collects parallels for a Greek word repeated in Aramaic or the reverse, Abaddon and Apollyon, and the old serpent called the Devil and Satan. Wesley makes it national rather than affectionate, holding that the Hebrew and Greek words are joined to express the joint cry of the Jews and the Gentiles. Robertson attends to the verb: the participle agrees with the neuter noun for Spirit by grammatical gender rather than in fact, and the word is an old, here rare, onomatopoetic term meaning to croak as a raven, covering any inarticulate cry like the unuttered groanings elsewhere which God understands.

Luther takes the sending of the Spirit as two things and cuts one off. In the primitive church, he says, the Holy Ghost was sent in a manifest and visible appearance, on Christ at Jordan in the likeness of a dove and on the Apostles in the likeness of fire; this was necessary then, since it was expedient that the church be established by many miracles because of the unbelievers, strange tongues being a sign not to them that believe but to them that believe not. But after the church was gathered and confirmed with those miracles, he concludes, it was not necessary that this visible sending continue any longer; the second sending, by the word into the hearts, remains.
7:
The shift from plural to singular is noticed by both the grammarians. Ellicott says the singular is used in order to individualise the expression and bring it home pointedly to each of the readers; Robertson says the same, that Paul changes to the singular to drive the point home to each one, since the spiritual experience has set each one free. Gill catalogues what is left behind, that in a natural state they were the servants of sin, the vassals of Satan, slaves to the world and its lusts and in bondage to the law, and are now freed from all of these, particularly from the law and the spirit of bondage it brought, being delivered by the spirit of adoption which enables them to cry Abba. Barnes and Clarke both give the shorter form of the same list, servitude to sin on the one hand and obligation to the Mosaic ritual on the other.

What the heirship consists in is where Clarke rises. This heirship, he says, is the most extraordinary of all: it is not an heirship of any tangible possession, either in heaven or earth, nor is it to possess a part or even the whole of either, but to possess Him who made all things — not God's works, but God himself. Wesley says the same more briefly, heir of all the promises and of the all-sufficient God himself. Ellicott grounds the inference in law rather than in rapture, noting that the Roman law, which the Apostle seems to be following, treated all the sons as heirs and provided for an equal division of the property between them; and he records a textual point, that the true reading here appears to be through God rather than through Christ, which he grants is a somewhat unusual expression.

Calvin qualifies the contrast he has been drawing all along. In the Christian Church, he says, slavery no longer exists but the condition of the children is free; yet the fathers under the law were slaves only in the sense that their freedom was not yet revealed but lay hidden under the coverings and yoke of the law. The ancients, he insists, were also sons of God and heirs through Christ, and we hold the same character but in a different manner, since we have Christ present with us and in that manner enjoy his blessings. Barnes reaches the same terminus by the shorter route, that the son is entitled to all the privileges of a son and so is to be regarded as an heir through the Redeemer and with him.

Luther turns the verse into a scene. The decree is pronounced in heaven, he writes, that there is no bondage any more but mere liberty and adoption; and when he asks who brings this liberty, his answer is the groaning itself. The Father offers by his promise his grace and his fatherly favour, and all that remains is that I should receive it, which is done when I again with this groaning cry and with a childly heart assent to the name of Father. There the Father and the Son meet, he says, and the marriage is made up without all pomp and solemnity, nothing at all coming between, no law nor work being required — for what, he asks, should a man do in these terrors and horrible darkness of temptations?
8:
Who is addressed here divides Clarke and Barnes. Barnes takes these verses to be evidently spoken to the Galatians who had been heathen, marking the transition by the adversative particle: the previous verses had the Jewish converts in view, and the Gentiles are now added as a condition of worse servitude still. Clarke grants that the great body of these churches were converts from among the Jews or proselytes, but says this verse shows some had come from heathenism, unless the Apostle addresses those who passed from heathenism into Judaism and thence into Christianity, which he thinks the likelier reading and the only one that makes the two verses consistent.

What the false gods were is answered twice. Ellicott notes that Paul elsewhere calls the gods of the heathen devils; Robertson gives the same reference, adding that Paul terms them the so-called gods, worshipped in images made by hands. Gill takes the clause more mildly, allowing that by the light of nature they might know there was a God but holding they did not know who he was, calling by that name mortal men, or stocks and stones and images of men's device. Henry adds that they were then under the worst of slaveries, serving those who, though accounted gods, were really no gods but mere creatures.

Calvin uses the comparison to sharpen a charge. This is no additional argument, he says, the point being already proved; the object is to make their fall appear more criminal. It is not wonderful that they went astray formerly, for wherever ignorance of God exists there must be dreadful blindness; but how disgraceful that in the midst of light they should fall into such gross errors. His inference is that they were less excusable for corrupting the gospel than for their old idolatry; and he adds the rule that until we are enlightened in the true knowledge of one God we always serve idols, whatever pretext we throw over the false religion.

The correction in the second verse is where everyone stops. Ellicott explains that the verb for knowing here differs from the one just used and brings out the process of coming to knowledge from previous ignorance; the correction follows because speaking of them as coming to know God might lay too much stress on the human side, true knowledge of God having for its converse the being known of God, that is, recognition and acceptance by him. Barnes says the same, that its object is to avoid the impression that their acquaintance with God was owing to themselves. Robertson notes the two participles as ingressive and passive forms of one verb, says Paul turns it round to the standpoint of God's elective grace, and calls the question that follows, in Bengel's phrase, a question full of wonder. Calvin, supplying parallels from the Greek writers for the corrective particles, says no language can express the base ingratitude of departing from God once known, which is to forsake of our own accord the light, the life and the fountain of all benefits.

Luther reads the correction as anxiety and then as doctrine. He fears they had lost God utterly, as if the Apostle said, alas, are ye come to this point, that now ye know not God but return from grace to the law, yet God knoweth you notwithstanding. From this he draws a principle: our knowledge is rather passive than active, consisting in this, that we are rather known of God than that we know him, so that all our endeavour to know God is to suffer God to work in us. Wesley reads the adjectives as a pair, weak because unable to purge the conscience from guilt, poor because incapable of enriching the soul with the holiness they are heirs to. Clarke puts it the same way, rites too weak to counteract sinful habits and too poor to purchase eternal life.
10:
Whether the Sabbath is among the observed days sets Barnes against everyone else. Gill takes the days to be the seventh-day sabbaths, distinguishing a religious observation from the civil division of time; Clarke says they superstitiously regard the sabbaths and days of their own appointment; Ellicott gives them as especially the Jewish sabbaths, Wesley simply as Jewish sabbaths. Barnes denies it outright: it is not a fair interpretation to suppose the apostle refers to the Sabbath properly so called, since that was part of the Decalogue and was observed by the Saviour himself and by the apostles; what is meant is the numerous Jewish festivals, including many the Jews had added to those of the Old Testament. Wesley draws a limit at the other end, that the years cannot mean sabbatic years, since these were not to be observed outside Canaan.

Ellicott notices that the list mounts in an ascending scale from days to months to seasons to years, and corrects the second term, which really means the new moon. Robertson attends to the verb, an old word meaning to stand beside and watch carefully, and adds that Paul knew the meticulous observance of the Pharisees to a nicety, so that it hurt him to the quick to see these Gentile Christians drawn into the spider-web of Judaizers, once set free and now enslaved again. Calvin guards the other side, that no condemnation is given here to the observance of dates in civil society, since the order of nature out of which this arises is fixed and constant.

The fear of the next verse is read as grammar by one man and as tactics by another. Robertson says Paul shudders to think of it, and observes that the construction is the usual one after a verb of fearing about what has actually happened, a future fear taking the subjunctive, so that Paul fears the worst has already come. Calvin calls the expression harsh and says it must have filled the Galatians with alarm, since what hope was left if Paul's labour had been in vain; it is the part of a wise pastor, he adds, to consider not what wanderers deserve but what is likeliest to bring them back.

What be as I am means nobody can settle, and Barnes says so. There is great brevity in the passage, he writes, and no little obscurity, and a great many different interpretations have been given; he lists Locke's, that you and I should be as if we were all one, and Koppe's, imitate my example, for I though a Jew by birth care no more for Jewish rites than you. Ellicott chooses the second, that Paul lays no stress on his Jewish descent and claims no privilege from circumcision, but stripped himself of all this and became a Gentile among Gentiles. Clarke offers both that and an affectionate reading, that they be as loving to him as he is to them. Henry takes the address as the point, that Paul styles them brethren though their hearts were largely alienated from him.

The illness that brought him there is inferred. Ellicott concludes that Paul was detained in Galatia accidentally by illness and that this led to his preaching there. Robertson agrees on the fact and refuses the diagnosis: all we can get is that the preaching was due to sickness of some kind, whether the eye trouble mentioned shortly after or the thorn in the flesh we do not know. Clarke resists the construction, allowing that the apostle was much afflicted when he first preached but insisting this may have been only an occasional affliction and not a continual and incurable infirmity, as some have too hastily conjectured. Calvin takes the word generally, of whatever made Paul appear mean and despised. Luther counts their reception of him the greatest benefit he had of them, his cross not offending them at all.
14:
The first clause turns on a variant, and all the critics report it. Gill notes that the Alexandrian copy and the Latin read your temptation in my flesh, meaning what was a trial to them, whether they would receive him. Barnes records the same variety, that Mill maintains your to be the true reading and Griesbach hesitates, but judges it unimportant, since on the other reading they were tempted by his infirmities to reject him. Clarke observes that the Greek word covers trial of any kind, so the verse may read either ye despised not the trial in my flesh or ye despised not your trial, meaning what his flesh suffered on their account. Ellicott states flatly that the true reading is your temptation in my flesh, Robertson translates it so, and Wesley reads it the other way, that they did not slight him for his temptation, which he identifies with the thorn in the flesh.

What the affliction was Ellicott will specify and Robertson will not. Ellicott identifies it with the thorn, or rather stake, in the flesh described elsewhere, notes that its effects appeared in the personal presence his enemies called mean, and concludes that an attack came on during the visit, so that he preached with health shattered by it. Robertson says only that the trial was a severe one, and turns to the verb for their not rejecting him, an old word meaning to spit out, found nowhere else in the New Testament; he reports Clemen's view that it should be taken literally, people having spat out as a prophylactic at the sight of invalids and especially epileptics, but notes that Plutarch uses it of mere rejection.

The next verse is grammatically unsettled, and Clarke says so bluntly: perhaps there is not a sentence in the New Testament more variously translated. He offers three renderings and notes that many manuscripts read where for what. Ellicott agrees that where has the strongest attestation and renders the noun as your felicitation of yourselves, asking what became of the loud assertions in which they once declared themselves blest. Barnes denies it is a question at all, taking it as an exclamation over that moment's happiness — what blessedness you had then, what overflowing joy. Wesley glosses it as that on which they once congratulated themselves.

Robertson notes that the offer of their eyes is a second-class condition with the usual particle unexpressed, calls it strong language saved from hyperbole by the qualification if possible, and raises without settling whether Paul then had eye trouble. Ellicott strikes the word own, laying the emphasis on the eyes. Luther reads it as praise beyond measure, that they would not only have plucked out their eyes but bestowed their lives; and they did bestow them, since by receiving a man the world accounted most execrable they turned on their own heads the hatred of Jews and Gentiles alike.

On the last question they agree in substance, differing in tone. Barnes turns it on the reader: how apt we are to feel that the man who tells us of our faults is our enemy, since he gives us pain, and we cannot have pain given us even by the stone we stumble against without some indignation. Robertson puts it in one line: it is always risky to speak the truth, the whole truth, since it may hit and hurt. Ellicott suggests the words may be a quotation, your enemy being what the Judaising teachers call him, and notes that the enemy was the name his opponents used in the next century. Calvin observes that though it is commonly said truth begets hatred, truth is never hateful except through the malice of those who cannot bear it. Luther makes Paul's defence for him: set these rebukes apart from the doctrine, applying the bitter potion not to your persons but to your disease.
17:
The verb Paul uses of the false teachers is neutral in itself. Barnes notes that it means to be zealous towards, for or against, usually in a good sense, and takes it here of a mere show of zeal to gain followers, as demagogues do who seek proselytes. Ellicott gives a run of renderings — to court, to curry favour with, to canvass eagerly. Robertson calls it an old and a good word, remarking that one can pay court with good motives or evil, and that against Paul's plain speech the Judaizers bring their fawning flattery. Clarke would render it that these false teachers endeavour to conciliate your esteem but not on honest principles. Gill and Calvin both note the omission of names, Gill saying the men were unworthy to have theirs transmitted to posterity, Calvin that Paul does more by silence to make them odious than if he had named them.

What the exclusion means divides them three ways. Clarke takes it of Paul himself, that they wish to shut the Galatians out from the affection of their apostle so that they might love and hear the newcomers alone, and Wesley the same, from Paul and from the gospel. Ellicott gives it a political sense, that they desire to separate the Galatians from the other Gentile churches and make Galatia an isolated centre of Judaism in which they may bear rule. Robertson makes it exclusion from Christ.

The concession about zeal is guarded. Barnes paraphrases it as a disclaimer, that Paul does not speak against zeal and would approve theirs in a good cause, and suspects they relied on it, as deceivers do, maintaining that zeal is itself sufficient evidence of a cause's goodness. Ellicott holds the proposition general so as to cover both sides; Calvin canvasses both and inclines to the Galatians.

The second birth is figured three ways. Robertson calls the word an old one for a powerful picture of pain and observes that Paul boldly represents himself as again the mother with birth pangs over them, the next verb giving the figure of an embryo developing into the child. Ellicott notes that the diminutive for children is not found elsewhere in Paul though common in John, adding that some of the best manuscripts read the simple form. Calvin says the diminutive expresses not contempt but endearment while suggesting the tender years of those who ought by now to be of full age, and that the style is abrupt, as usually in highly pathetic passages, since strong feeling breaks off our words half uttered. Luther calls it an allegory, the Apostles standing in the place of parents, for as parents beget the bodily form so they beget the form of the mind, and the form of a Christian mind is faith. Wesley glosses the end of the travail as all the mind that was in Christ being in them.

The wish to be present is taken as an admission of helplessness. Robertson renders the imperfect as I was just wishing, notes that Paul could put his heart into his voice but that the pen now stands between them, and glosses the closing verb as being at a loss. Ellicott renders it I could indeed wish, changes voice to tone, and explains the perplexity as not knowing how to deal with them so as to win them back. Clarke says he wishes to accommodate his doctrine to their state, not knowing whether they need stronger reprehension or gentler dealing. Calvin calls it the complaint of a father so perplexed by his sons' misconduct that he looks about for advice and knows not to what hand to turn. Henry contrasts him with the false teachers, that he was not one thing among them and another when absent. Luther reads the passage as a lively description of an apostle's true affection, chiding, entreating, and commending their faith.
21:
The word for law shifts sense inside a single question, and Clarke says so outright: first the Mosaic institutions, and then the Pentateuch, where the history he is about to use is recorded. Barnes agrees the second use is not the commands uttered at Sinai but the book, since the Jews classed all five books of Moses under that name. Gill guards the first use: all believers desire to be under the law as holy, just and good, but these men sought justification by their obedience and so desired it as a covenant of works, which was the way to come under its curse. Calvin defines it as coming under the yoke on the condition that God act toward you according to the covenant of the law and you bind yourself to keep it; in any other sense, he says, all believers are under the law. Ellicott takes the verb for hearing as giving heed, and mentions the alternative that it merely refers to the synagogue practice of reading a lesson; Henry simply assumes they did hear it, since among the Jews it was read every sabbath day. Robertson sees them on the point of surrender to legalism and calls Paul's turn surprising but legitimate.

Whether the allegory is in the text or only in the use divides them. Henry allows that beyond the literal sense the Spirit of God might design to signify something further. Barnes denies it flatly: he does not suppose the narrative was designed to represent the two conditions, and holds that Paul uses it as any one may use a striking historical fact to illustrate a principle. Calvin threads between them. He says Paul certainly does not mean that Moses wrote the history for the purpose of being turned into an allegory, but points out in what way it answers the present subject; and since the house of Abraham was then a true Church, its principal events are so many types to us. The digression that follows is his sharpest: Origen and many others seized this word to torture Scripture, until for many centuries no man was thought ingenious who lacked the daring to change the sacred word into a variety of curious shapes. He calls this a contrivance of Satan, and insists the true meaning is the natural and obvious one. Luther makes the same limit: allegories do not strongly persuade in divinity but as certain pictures they beautify the matter, and as painting garnishes a house already built, so an allegory lights a matter otherwise proved.

On the two sons the difference is located differently. Luther presses that both were true sons, of one father, one flesh, one seed, and that what divides them is not the mother's status, though that pertains to the allegory, but that Ishmael was born without the promise and the word of God — Sarah gave her maid at her own suggestion, with no word commanding it, so that he was born at adventure. Clarke and Wesley locate it in nature: after the flesh means naturally, and since both Abraham and Sarah had passed the age at which procreation was naturally possible, Isaac's birth was supernatural and credible only on the ground of the promise, by that strength given in consequence of it. Ellicott makes the promise itself creative, the birth due to its direct agency. Calvin puts it in election, nothing besides nature in Ishmael and the choice of God in Isaac, with an indirect reference to the calling of the Gentiles. Barnes reads condition rather than miracle throughout: the son of the slave was inferior from his very birth, no promise attending him, servitude following him through his whole life. The word for bondmaid is a feminine diminutive of the word for boy or slave; Ellicott adds it was not confined to that sense in earlier Greek but used of any young girl.
24:
Everyone agrees the word means one thing said by another, and nearly all hedge it. Gill calls allegory a continued metaphor and notes that Philo had allegorised Sarah and Hagar first. Robertson calls the verb late and found only here in the New Testament and holds that Paul does not deny the narrative but puts a secondary meaning on it; he adds that preachers in Alexandria carried Philo's method to excess, a style that survives yet to the discredit of sound preaching. Barnes denies any such design in Moses and says Paul uses the story as the Saviour used his parables. Ellicott holds that the allegorical sense does not exclude the literal but is added to it, denies Paul uses the word in the strict sense that would make the narrative fictitious, and quotes Calvin by name for the justification, while insisting the force of the passage rests on the assertion of Christian liberty, not on the inference. Clarke thinks Paul borrowed the method from Jewish writings to convict the Judaizers on their own principles, but ends with an imprecation on the vain and superficial minds who find allegories everywhere, whose spiritualizing he calls more properly carnalizing.

The two covenants are read as two mothers. Calvin chose covenant over testament to keep the comparison, a neuter noun sounding harsh for a mother, and makes doctrine the mother of whom we are born, twofold, legal and evangelical. He raises the objection himself, that none of God's children are born to slavery, and answers that under the veil of ceremonies the freedom of the holy fathers was concealed, so that to the outward eye nothing but slavery appeared, and that the children of Sinai here meant are hypocrites who abuse the law. Clarke and Wesley take the two as two systems of religion, one by Moses and one by the Messiah, and Clarke presses that as a bondmaid could bring forth only into slavery, so those under Moses must keep the whole law yet live in habitual breach of it. Ellicott glosses the verb as standing for, comparing the interpretation of the tares and the words at the supper.

Whether Hagar is really an Arabic name for Sinai is the sharpest dispute here. Luther reports that the Arabians call the mountain by that name and that it signifies a handmaid, and thinks the likeness gave Paul occasion to seek out the allegory. Gill offers the same philology from another angle, the word denoting a rock, one part of the country being called Arabia Petraea from its rockiness. Ellicott devotes an excursus to it and concludes for it. Barnes refuses it: he cannot find in Castell or Gesenius that the word bears that sense in Arabic, still less that Paul knew of it, and falls back on the rule that the plainest sense is generally the true one. He reports that Bentley proposed to cancel the clause as an interpolation, and Clarke that respectable manuscripts omit the name altogether. Calvin calls Jerome's conjecture of two names trifling, and adds that the situation is mentioned by way of contempt, lying beyond the limits of the holy land.

On the word for answering, three reach for parallel columns. Ellicott calls it a technical term for the columns of antithetical pairs, so that Hagar, Sinai and the earthly Jerusalem stand in one line. Robertson gives it a military origin, keeping step in line, and cites Lightfoot on the Pythagorean table of opposites. Calvin denies it means nearness or position and compares Aristotle's calling rhetoric the counterpart of logic. Luther's comment is an admission against his own instinct: he would gladly have made Jerusalem into Sarah, since the gospel began there and the Spirit was given there — but Paul joins her to Sinai, from which he concludes that allegory is not for every man to use at pleasure, since a goodly outward show may deceive.
26:
Where the Jerusalem above is to be found gets three answers. Barnes and Ellicott take it celestially, Barnes using the city to denote the church as of heavenly origin, Ellicott making it the seat of the Messianic kingdom, a spiritual city of which the Christian is a member here and now. Calvin denies the spatial reading outright: it is not contained in heaven, nor to be sought out of this world, since the Church is spread over the whole earth and is a stranger and pilgrim on it; it is called heavenly because it originates in heavenly grace. Gill narrows it in time rather than place, taking it not of the church triumphant but of the gospel church state under the new covenant, and not as in the latter-day glory when the new city shall descend, but as it then was, with particular respect to the first church at Jerusalem. Clarke supplies the rabbinic maxim that whatsoever was on earth was found also in heaven; Robertson says Paul uses that idea without endorsing it, and adds that the city stands for the whole Jewish race.

On the mother of us all, Clarke calls the word for all spurious, omitted by almost every ancient manuscript and father, and prints the clause without it; Ellicott agrees. What it underwrites divides them. Barnes and Wesley keep it to persons — all true Christians, whether by birth Jews or Gentiles, free citizens of the new city. Calvin builds an ecclesiology on it: to the Church we owe it that we are born again of incorruptible seed, so that he who refuses to be a son of the Church in vain desires to have God for his Father. He then turns the same words against Rome, calling those who quote them fools and twice children and their mother an adulteress who brings forth to death the children of the devil, and observing that the synagogue could have claimed as much with higher plausibility, yet Paul consigns her to the lot of Hagar. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the phrase the other way, using it of the one Holy Catholic Church and warning the catechumen that in a strange city he must not ask simply where the Lord's House is, since the sects also call their own dens houses of the Lord, but where the Catholic Church is.

The prophecy is quoted for the ingathering. Gill takes it as proof that the gospel church state has brought forth more souls than the legal dispensation did. Barnes says the object is to prove that Gentiles as well as Jews share the privilege, notes that Paul quotes the Greek version rather than the Hebrew, and calls the accession from the heathen world a prophecy already fulfilled. Clarke and Wesley read it the same way, the desolate being the Gentile nations destitute for many ages of a seed to serve the Lord and the woman with a husband the Jewish state long in covenant. Ellicott layers it in three: the ruined post-exilic city against Jerusalem in its prosperity, Sarah against Hagar, and Christianity with its small beginnings against the old dispensation. Calvin makes the design polemical, to deprive the Jews of all claim to that spiritual city, whose children are gathered out of all nations by free grace and no preparation of hers. Robertson calls it a song of triumph looking for deliverance from a foreign yoke, glosses the second verb as to rend or burst asunder with joy to be supplied, and remarks that Paul's thought moves rapidly but never loses its line. Luther traces the oracle back to the song of Hannah, where the bow of the mighty is broken and the weak girded with strength, and reads the fruitful woman as the synagogue with the law for her husband, begetting children who shine in works and are nevertheless bondservants.
28:
Two of them pause over what kind of move the application is. Henry admits that no reader would have found this allegory in the history unless it had been shown him, yet does not doubt the Spirit intended it, and calls it an explanation of the subject and not an argument in proof of it; Barnes rests his conclusion on the same ground, since Paul does not use the allegory as an argument. Ellicott thinks the better reading is ye rather than we, Robertson notes the same variation without letting it change the sense, and Gill reports it too. Barnes puts the resemblance in the promises made to us and the contrast in Ishmael, to whom none was made; Wesley makes it birth by the supernatural power of God, Clarke the offspring of the Messiah.

What Ishmael actually did is disputed by those most careful with the Hebrew. Ellicott doubts whether the word means more than playing, though our version renders it mocking, and reports the tradition that Ishmael took the child out and shot at him with arrows under pretence of sport. Robertson notes the Hebrew has laughing where the Greek has mocking, and repeats it. Calvin is the most exacting: persecution is nowhere mentioned, only that Ishmael ridiculed his brother; the explanation that this was a simple smile is inadmissible, since no cruelty would be argued by so fearfully revenging a harmless smile, so that he must have provoked the child with reproachful language — and yet, Calvin asks, how far is this from persecution? He turns to the present, where the children of the law molest the sons of God over outward ceremonies with their father's disdain. Clarke extends it to the Jews who everywhere persecute Christians and so show themselves of the posterity of Hagar, Wesley to all ages and nations to the end of the world. Barnes brings evidence, citing Paley that Paul was never set upon by Gentiles unless the Jews stirred them up first, excepting Philippi and Ephesus. Luther takes the harder objection, that all was peaceful before the gospel came abroad and now the world is in an uproar, and answers that the faithful must bear the name of schismatics.

The expulsion is quoted as Scripture though the words are Sarah's. Gill notes the formula of citation is Talmudic, and that since she spoke under inspiration and God confirmed her the words are ascribed to God speaking in the Scripture; Ellicott and Robertson both note the endorsement. Who is to be cast out divides them. Barnes denies the command means expelling the Judaising teachers from Galatia, taking it of servitude itself, and adds that Paul cannot mean the passage originally referred to the gospel, nothing being farther from Sarah's mind. The others read a sentence upon persons: Clarke that the present Jerusalem is cast out of the favour of God, Wesley that God will cast out all who seek justification by the law, Luther that it overthrows as many as trust in their own works and judge us to be heretics cast out of the church. Luther alone pauses over Abraham, to whom the thing was very grievous until God confirmed the sentence. Ellicott calls the declaration a bold assertion of the incompatibility of Judaism with Christianity, and Robertson quotes Lightfoot that the law must disappear before the gospel. Calvin turns the whole to consolation, that the tyranny of the Ishmaelites will not last for ever and those who now look down on us will one day be declared the sons of a slave, so that we should not fret because of evil-doers who hold a temporary rank in the Church; he grants that if we simply call our opponents Ishmaelites they will smile at us. Barnes closes on the birthright of Christians to think and act like freemen, Luther on the liberty purchased by Christ as a strong fort.
